entry.title: Stop Using a Language Model for Everything. Here’s What I Use Instead.

link.title: Stop Using a Language Model for Everything. Here’s What I Use Instead.

entry.content:
Most enterprise agent pipelines have the same assumption baked in from the start: the AI layer is an LLM, every call goes through it, and the question is just which one. I built a production pipeline with that assumption and ran it long enough to start questioning it.

When I profiled the call breakdown, roughly 80% of the AI work was structured decision-making. Classify this intent. Score this document for relevance. Extract these fields from an unstructured input. None of those outputs were ever read by a human. They fed directly into the next system. I was paying frontier LLM prices and tolerating LLM latency for tasks that didn’t need generative capability at all. And occasionally the model would invent a field that wasn’t in the input, because nothing in its architecture prevents that.

That’s what prompted me to evaluate Jev, released in September 2026 by TypeSafe AI, founded by Diogo Almeida (formerly OpenAI).

What System One Models Actually Are

LLMs are trained with RLHF. The optimization target is outputs human raters prefer, which makes them excellent at generation and structurally overconfident. Uncertain answers score poorly with human raters even when uncertainty is the accurate state. The output is always a string. Your code parses it, validates it, and lives with the fact that there’s always a path where the model produces well-formatted nonsense.

Jev uses RLCD, Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions. You define the output schema in advance. The model selects from that space and returns a typed value with a calibrated confidence score. There’s no generative step. The model cannot produce an output that violates the schema because the schema is the entire output space. TypeSafe describes it as “a frontier-intelligence function call: unstructured state in, typed probabilistic decisions out.”

The calibration is as important as the typing. An LLM prompted to express confidence tends to express consistent confidence, not accurate confidence. Calibrated means when Jev reports 90% confidence, it’s right 90% of the time statistically across those calls. That becomes a real architectural control surface: you set the threshold for autonomous action versus escalation, and the threshold is meaningful.

The Two-Stack Architecture

Most real agent pipelines have two kinds of work running through the same model class: decision-making at the edges and synthesis at the core. Separating them is what makes the cost and latency gap meaningful.

flowchart TD
    A([Incoming Query]) --> B["Jev: Intent Classification\n70–500ms · $0.042/MTok"]
    B --> C{Confidence\nScore}
    C -->|"> 0.85 · High confidence"| D[Route Directly\nStructured action]
    C -->|"< 0.85 · Low confidence"| E[Escalate to LLM\nClaude / GPT]
    E --> F[Synthesis + Generation\nOutput a human reads]
    D --> G([Pipeline continues])
    F --> G

The confidence threshold is the key architectural lever. With an LLM, “escalate if unsure” requires prompt engineering and hoping the model accurately signals its own uncertainty. With Jev, it’s a numeric cutoff on calibrated output. You set it, it’s testable, it’s consistent.

What This Looks Like in Code

Here’s a routing step from a RAG intake pipeline. The before version uses an LLM to classify whether an incoming query needs retrieval:

# Before: LLM call, parse string, hope it says yes or no
response = claude.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Does this query need retrieval? {query}"}]
)
needs_retrieval = "yes" in response.content[0].text.lower()

The failure mode here is invisible: the model parses and responds in ways that look right and aren’t. It might say “Yes, retrieval is needed” or “Retrieval would be appropriate here” or add caveats that break the parse. The Jev version:

# After: Jev typed decision with calibrated confidence
result = jev.decide(
    input=query,
    schema={
        "needs_retrieval": {"type": "bool"},
        "category": {"type": "enum", "values": ["billing", "technical", "general"]}
    }
)
if result.confidence > 0.85:
    route_autonomously(result.needs_retrieval, result.category)
else:
    escalate_to_llm(query)

The difference isn’t just cleaner code. The schema fails loudly at definition time, not silently at runtime. And the confidence gate is a real signal, not a parsed string.

The Cost and Latency Gap

Frontier LLMs run $0.20 to $10 per million input tokens with response times of 3 to 329 seconds. Jev is $0.042 per million tokens, responds in 70 to 500ms, and output tokens are free.

For classification, routing, and structured extraction workloads, that’s roughly 100x cheaper and 40 to 200x faster. TypeSafe published results from Jack and Jill, a hiring platform: they replaced an LLM-based candidate screening pipeline with Jev and got 88% cost reduction, 2x throughput, and 10 days from test to production.

The Decision Rule

If the AI call ends with a human reading the output, use an LLM. If it ends with your code acting on the output, evaluate Jev first.

The second category is larger than most architects realize. Routing, intent classification, entity extraction, confidence gating, relevance scoring. These are all structured decision tasks running at LLM prices inside most pipelines today, not because they need generative capability but because LLMs are the default reach.

The enterprise AI conversation has spent two years on which LLM vendor to use. For the decision-making workload inside a real agent pipeline, that’s the wrong question. The question is which model class.

entry.title: Harness Engineering and Loop Engineering: The Layer Between an LLM and Real Work

link.title: Harness Engineering and Loop Engineering: The Layer Between an LLM and Real Work

entry.content:
First, what is an AI agent? The term gets thrown around loosely. It’s a language model (an LLM, the kind of AI behind ChatGPT or Claude) that does more than answer a question once. It can take actions such as reading a file, running a command or searching the web, look at what happened, and decide what to do next, in a loop, until the task is done. A chatbot takes one input and gives one output. An agent can keep acting, unsupervised, for as long as it takes.

That’s what makes agents useful, and also what makes them risky. Prompt engineering is about wording your instructions so a model gives a good answer in a single response. That’s necessary, but it isn’t enough once the model is acting on its own, reading its own results, deciding what to do next and deciding when to stop. At that point a second discipline appears. The question changes from “what do I say to the model?” to “what do I build around it?”

I call the two halves harness engineering and loop engineering. People often lump both together as “the agent,” but they’re different things.

  • The harness is everything the model is allowed to do, which tools it can call, what files it can touch, what commands are off-limits, how much context it sees before it even starts.
  • The loop is the control flow that keeps calling the model, checking what it wants to do, letting it (or not), feeding the result back, and deciding when to stop.

Get the harness wrong and a capable model can do dangerous or useless things simply because nobody told it not to. Get the loop wrong and a well-behaved model can still run forever, burn through your budget, or drift off the original task because nothing was watching for it.

This post explains both from first principles, then walks through one example: an agent that auto-fixes failing tests in a pull request. I’ll use Claude Code (permission modes, hooks, subagents, on-demand tool loading and CLAUDE.md instructions) as the running reference, since I use it every day.

A few terms

If you’ve built with LLM APIs before, skip this. If not, these five terms come up a lot:

  • Context window, the total amount of text (measured in tokens, roughly word-fragments) a model can “see” at once, including its instructions, the conversation so far, and anything it just read. It’s finite, usually a few hundred thousand tokens, and everything you put in it costs money and pushes out room for something else.
  • System prompt, a block of instructions given to the model before the conversation starts, setting its role, rules, and boundaries. The user never sees it directly; it shapes how the model behaves throughout.
  • Tool call / tool use, when a model, instead of just replying with text, asks to run a specific action, “call the Bash tool with this command”, and waits for the result before continuing. This is the mechanism that turns a chatbot into an agent.
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol), a standard way to plug external systems (Slack, a database, Google Drive) into an agent as tools, without writing custom integration code for each one.
  • Sandbox, a restricted environment (limited filesystem access, no network, a disposable container) that limits what a tool call can actually affect, even if the model asks for something dangerous.

Two failure modes

The easiest way to see why they’re separate is to look at what breaks when you skip each one.

Skip the harness and the model has no boundaries. It can call any tool with any argument, read files outside the project, run destructive shell commands or leak sensitive output. It isn’t malicious. Nothing told it not to. I call this a scope failure: it did something it should never have been allowed to try.

Skip the loop design and the model has boundaries but no brakes. It re-reads the same file five times, retries a failing action endlessly, or keeps going “one more turn” until the conversation has been summarised so many times that it forgets what it was asked to do. I call this a termination failure: each action was allowed, but nothing made it stop.

Most prompt engineering advice is about the small “Model” circle in the middle. In my experience, most of the reliability problems in real agent systems are in everything else in the picture.

What a harness is made of

The harness is everything that’s true about the model’s environment before it generates a single word. It’s like onboarding a contractor: before they touch anything, you’ve decided which systems they can log into, which files they can edit and who has to approve what. The harness is that setup, written down and enforced in code. For a coding agent like Claude Code it looks roughly like this:

Five boxes, five jobs:

  • Context Assembly, what information the model gets to see before it starts working: its instructions, any project-specific rules, anything remembered from before.
  • Tool Surface, the full list of actions the model is even capable of requesting. If a tool isn’t in this list, the model can’t call it, period, this is the first and strongest form of control.
  • Permission Gate, for tools that are available, whether a specific call is allowed to actually run, or needs a human to approve it first.
  • Hooks, small pieces of code that run automatically before or after a tool call, regardless of what the model “intended.”
  • State & Isolation, what gets remembered between turns, and what stays walled off between separate agents working at the same time.

Three of these deserve a closer look, because they’re the parts people tend to skip when building their own harness.

Deferred tool loading

Every tool comes with a description (its “schema”): its name, its arguments and what it does. The model can only use what’s in its context window, so if you describe forty tools in full, you pay for all forty on every turn, whether or not they’re used. It’s like making a new employee re-read the whole handbook before every task instead of pointing them to the one page they need.

Claude Code handles this by showing the model only tool names by default and loading the full description once a tool looks necessary:

# What the model sees by default — just names, cheap to include:
CronCreate, CronDelete, WebFetch, SendMessage, ... (names only)

# Only after the model asks for one specifically:
ToolSearch("select:WebFetch") → full parameter schema, now callable

This matters more as the tool list grows. MCP makes it easy to add a dozen integrations, and without deferred loading every one of their descriptions sits in every prompt, even when the task has nothing to do with Slack or a database.

Permission modes

The simplest harness is binary: the model can do anything, or it must ask about everything. The first is reckless and the second is so irritating that people switch it off. Claude Code has a few modes in between: default (ask before risky actions), acceptEdits (auto-approve file edits, ask about the rest), plan (read and research only) and bypassPermissions (no asking). It’s a dial you set based on how much you trust the agent and how bad a mistake would be. A file edit and a git push --force are not the same risk, so they shouldn’t need the same approval.

Hooks

You can tell a model in its instructions not to run destructive commands, and it will usually listen. “Usually” is the problem. A hook is a small script that runs before a tool executes (a PreToolUse hook) and can block the call whatever the model decided. That matters wherever “usually” isn’t good enough: compliance requirements, sensitive repositories, audit trails. A prompt instruction is a request. A hook is a rule the code enforces whether the model agrees or not.

What a loop is made of

If the harness is the walls, the loop is what happens inside them: call the model, see what it wants to do, act on it if allowed, feed the result back, and repeat until there’s nothing left to do or a limit is hit.

In words: the model is called and replies with a stop_reason, a label saying why it stopped generating. If it’s end_turn, the model has a final answer and you return it. If it’s tool_use, the model wants to run something, and that’s when the permission check from the harness is consulted. If denied, the model is told so (as a tool_result, the standard way to feed an outcome back) and tries something else. If allowed, the tool runs, the result is appended to the conversation, and the loop goes round again, unless a budget or cost limit has been hit, in which case it stops and escalates to a human.

The permission check and the budget check are, to me, the heart of it. The rest is plumbing.

A minimal loop in code

Production frameworks add a lot of ceremony, but the core is small enough to read in one go:

def run_loop(client, system_prompt, tools, user_message, max_iterations=25):
    # messages is the running conversation — every model reply and every
    # tool result gets appended here, and the whole thing is sent back
    # to the model on the *next* call so it has full context of what happened.
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_message}]

    for iteration in range(max_iterations):
        # One call to the model. It sees the system prompt (its instructions),
        # the tools it's allowed to request, and the conversation so far.
        response = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-sonnet-5",
            system=system_prompt,
            tools=tools,
            messages=messages,
        )
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return response  # model gave a final answer — end_turn — we're done

        # The model wants to run one or more tools. Each one shows up as a
        # separate "tool_use" block inside response.content.
        tool_results = []
        for block in response.content:
            if block.type != "tool_use":
                continue

            decision = check_permission(block.name, block.input)  # harness boundary
            if decision == "denied":
                result = f"Denied: {block.name} is not permitted in this context"
            else:
                result = execute_tool(block.name, block.input)    # harness boundary

            # tool_result tells the model what happened — success, failure,
            # or a denial reason — so it can decide what to do on the next turn.
            tool_results.append({
                "type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": block.id,
                "content": result,
            })

        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results})

    # We reached the iteration cap without the model ever giving a final
    # answer — that's the loop's safety valve, not an edge case to ignore.
    raise IterationBudgetExceeded(f"No terminal response after {max_iterations} turns")

Note what’s missing: retry logic, summarising old messages, cost tracking and spawning other agents. A production harness needs all of those, but each hooks into this loop at one narrow point: the check_permission call, the execute_tool call or the iteration limit. Don’t build them before the basic loop works. A simple loop with a hardcoded cap and a basic permission check that terminates correctly beats an elaborate one that doesn’t.

Subagents

Once the basic loop works, the next question is what to do when a task is too big for one context window, or should be kept apart from the main conversation. A code reviewer shouldn’t see the author’s back-and-forth, and a research task shouldn’t fill the main thread with dozens of search results.

Claude Code, like most serious multi-agent systems, answers by doing the same thing again at a smaller scale. A subagent is a second, independent harness-plus-loop, with its own tools, permission checks, iteration budget and conversation history, which the parent agent invokes like any other tool.

Two details matter here. First, fresh context: the subagent starts with no memory of the parent’s conversation, only what it’s explicitly given. Second, the parent gets back only the subagent’s final report, not its turn-by-turn transcript.

That choice does real work. Worktree isolation, giving each subagent its own copy of the files, stops parallel agents overwriting each other’s changes. Hiding the intermediate steps keeps the parent’s context window from filling up. It’s the same idea I used in the pipeline from my earlier post: each stage received only the finished output of the previous one, never its raw conversation. In practice harness and loop engineering aren’t really separable. They’re one design decision seen from two sides.

Where this breaks in practice

Unbounded loops that look like thoroughness. Given a broad task and no cap, a model will happily read every file in a large project “to be thorough.” Wanting more context isn’t the bug. Nothing stopping it is. An iteration cap is the loop’s real safety valve, not an afterthought, and it should scale with risk: a read-only subagent can reasonably get more turns than one that can delete or overwrite things.

Tool schema bloat. Each MCP integration adds tool descriptions to the context. Past a point, a new tool costs more in context than it adds in capability, and it raises the odds of the model picking the wrong tool among many similar ones. On-demand loading is the fix, rather than simply having fewer tools, since you often do need the capability, just not paid for on every turn.

Permission checks that only look at the tool name. Bash isn’t one risk level. ls and rm -rf are both “the Bash tool.” A harness that checks only which tool is called, and not what it’s asked to do, ends up too permissive (allow all Bash) or too annoying (ask about every call). The permission layer has to look at the arguments.

Losing the “why” in compaction. When a long conversation outgrows the context window, older parts are summarised to make room. This is compaction. It’s easy for the summary to keep what happened (files touched, commands run) and lose why (the reasoning that ruled out another approach earlier). A summary that’s just an action log makes the loop retry things it already rejected. Good compaction keeps the reasoning.

Confusing “the model refused” with “the harness blocked it.” They can look identical in a transcript but need opposite fixes. If the model is declining something reasonable, that’s a prompt problem. If a hook or permission rule is silently blocking something it shouldn’t, that’s a harness bug, and it’s easy to blame the model when the fix is in your PreToolUse hook.

A worked example: a CI auto-fix agent

Here’s one concrete scenario, the kind of agent teams reach for early: watch a pull request’s failing tests (CI, continuous integration) and have the agent push a fix.

What the naive version does

The naive build takes twenty minutes. Give the model three tools: Bash (run shell commands), Edit (modify a file) and Write (create a file). The system prompt says “Fix the failing tests in this PR. Don’t touch unrelated code.” Wrap it in a loop that runs until the model says it’s done.

Here’s what I’d expect on the first real pull request, as opposed to a clean demo:

  1. It runs forever. One failing test is flaky, failing intermittently for reasons unrelated to the code. The model “fixes” it, the flake comes back, the model reverts its fix, the test passes by chance, the model declares victory, and the flake returns on the next run. Forty turns later it’s still flipping between two versions of one function.
  2. It edits files outside the PR. Nothing enforces “don’t touch unrelated code.” The instruction works only if the model happens to follow it. It spots an unrelated warning two files over and cleans it up while it’s there, and a two-line fix now touches eleven files.
  3. It runs a destructive command. To get a clean starting point, it runs git checkout ., which discards all uncommitted changes, including a colleague’s unsaved work in the same workspace.

None of this is mysterious misbehaviour. Each is a specific missing control, and each maps to something earlier in this post:

Failure Missing control Which side
Runs forever, oscillates No stop condition beyond “the model says it’s done” Loop
Edits unrelated files No check on what Edit/Write is actually touching Harness
Destructive git command No check on what the Bash command actually says Harness

The fixes

None of this needs a new framework. The permission check and the stop condition just have to inspect what’s actually happening instead of trusting the prompt:

  • Restrict Edit/Write to the files the PR already changes. Anything else is denied before it runs.
  • Check the actual Bash command text. Match every command against a deny-list of destructive patterns such as rm -rf, git push --force, git checkout . and git reset --hard.
  • Replace “the model says it’s done” with a progress signal. Track how many tests fail after each attempt. If the number hasn’t dropped over the last few tries, the loop is stuck, not thorough. Stop and hand it to a human.

Building it

Both checks are plain deterministic code, not another model call, so they’re cheap enough to run on every tool call.

The scope check plugs into the same check_permission step as the minimal loop. It runs before a tool executes, so a bad call never happens:

import re

# Only files this specific PR already modifies — computed once, up front,
# from the PR's diff. Nothing outside this list is in scope.
ALLOWED_PATHS = get_changed_files(pr_diff)

# Regex patterns matched against the literal command string before it runs.
DANGEROUS_COMMANDS = [
    r"rm\s+-rf",              # recursive, forced delete
    r"git\s+push\s+.*--force", # overwrites remote history
    r"git\s+checkout\s+\.",    # discards all local uncommitted changes
    r"git\s+reset\s+--hard",   # discards all local changes and history
]

def check_permission(tool_name, tool_input):
    if tool_name in ("Edit", "Write"):
        path = tool_input["file_path"]
        if path not in ALLOWED_PATHS:
            return "denied", f"{path} is outside this PR's changed-file scope"

    if tool_name == "Bash":
        command = tool_input["command"]
        if any(re.search(pattern, command) for pattern in DANGEROUS_COMMANDS):
            return "denied", f"blocked destructive command: {command}"

    return "allowed", None

The progress check lives in the loop itself and runs after each tool result. The only new state is failure_counts, a list of how many tests failed after each attempt:

def run_ci_fix_loop(client, system_prompt, tools, pr_context, max_iterations=15):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": pr_context}]
    failure_counts = []

    for iteration in range(max_iterations):
        response = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-sonnet-5", system=system_prompt, tools=tools, messages=messages
        )
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return response

        tool_results = []
        for block in response.content:
            if block.type != "tool_use":
                continue

            decision, reason = check_permission(block.name, block.input)
            if decision == "denied":
                result = f"Denied: {reason}"
            else:
                result = execute_tool(block.name, block.input)
                # Every time the agent runs the test suite, record how many
                # tests are still failing — this is the progress signal.
                if block.name == "Bash" and "pytest" in block.input.get("command", ""):
                    failure_counts.append(count_failures(result))

            tool_results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": result})

        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results})

        # If the last 3 test runs show the exact same failure count,
        # the agent isn't making progress — it's stuck, not being thorough.
        if len(failure_counts) >= 3 and len(set(failure_counts[-3:])) == 1:
            escalate_to_human(reason="no progress in last 3 test runs", transcript=messages)
            return None

    escalate_to_human(reason="iteration budget exceeded", transcript=messages)

A backup for destructive commands lives outside the Python entirely, as a hook, so a bug in check_permission doesn’t remove the protection:

// .claude/settings.json — enforced regardless of what the loop code does
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "scripts/block-destructive-git.sh" }]
      }
    ]
  }
}

That’s defence in depth rather than duplication. The two checks are separate pieces of code, so a mistake in one leaves the other intact.

What changes

On the flaky-test PR, the progress check fires after three flat test runs instead of forty turns of back-and-forth. On the “clean up this unrelated file” case, the Edit is denied before it touches disk and the model is told why, so it adjusts. On git checkout ., the command is blocked twice, once by the argument check and once by the hook, and there’s a record of what was attempted.

Same task, same model, same prompt. The only difference is that the harness and loop no longer assume the prompt alone will keep the model in line.

Closing thoughts

Prompt engineering tunes a single response. Harness and loop engineering are about a system that takes many actions on its own. In theory they’re separate: the harness is what’s allowed, the loop is how long it runs and when it stops. In practice they’re tightly linked, because the things you care about in production (bounded cost, bounded blast radius, loud failures instead of silent ones, being able to recover from a mistake) are all enforced where the two meet.

If you build on an existing harness like Claude Code or the Claude Agent SDK, the work doesn’t disappear. It moves. You won’t write check_permission by hand, but you will write settings.json rules, hooks and CLAUDE.md scope. You won’t write the iteration cap, but you will decide subagent boundaries and what information crosses them.

If you’re building your first agent, start with the permission boundary and the stop condition, before the prompt. Everything else is easier to fix once those two are solid.
entry.summary: First, what is an AI agent? The term gets thrown around loosely. It’s a language model (an LLM, the kind of AI behind ChatGPT or Claude) that does more than answer a question once. It can take actions such as reading a file, running a command or searching the web, look at what happened, and decide what to do next, in a loop, until the task is done. A chatbot takes one input and gives one output. An agent can keep acting, unsupervised, for as long as it takes.

entry.title: SDLC Factory: Autonomous Software Delivery with AI Agents

link.title: SDLC Factory: Autonomous Software Delivery with AI Agents

entry.content:
Software delivery loses information at every handoff. An idea starts out clear in someone’s head, goes through six meetings, three Confluence pages and a Jira backlog nobody reads, and ends up as code that solves last quarter’s version of the problem. Even good teams lose time and detail at each boundary between product, architecture, development and QA.

Over the last few months I’ve been building something to attack this: SDLC Factory. It takes a plain-English product idea and drives it through a full delivery pipeline using 10 specialised AI agents, enforced artifact contracts between stages, and human approval gates at the points that matter.

It’s more than a chatbot wrapper. It has parallel development threads, a QA auto-fix loop, context compression for long conversations, prompt injection scanning, multi-tenant isolation and a cost tracker. This post covers how I built it, the design decisions that mattered, and what I got wrong the first time.

What’s wrong with the usual approaches

Most AI coding agents I’ve seen fall into one of two camps:

  1. Single-agent loops. One model does everything: requirements, design, code and tests. It forgets what it decided three pages ago and writes code that doesn’t match its own spec.
  2. Unstructured multi-agent systems. Agents spawn sub-agents freely and coordinate in natural language. It sounds powerful, but in my experience the coordination overhead eats the gains and debugging is painful.

Neither guarantees that the output of one stage is valid input for the next. Requirements drift from the architecture, and the architecture drifts from the code. There’s no contract.

SDLC Factory enforces one. Every stage produces a JSON artifact validated against a schema, and the next stage gets only what it needs from earlier stages. It never sees the raw conversation history.

System architecture

Here’s how the whole system fits together:

Seven Stages, Ten Agents

The Agent Contract

The agent hierarchy is the core abstraction. Every role declares exactly what it needs, what tools it can use, and what it must produce:

Every subclass declares:

  • OUTPUT_SCHEMA, JSON Schema that the runtime validates the artifact against before advancing
  • ENABLED_TOOLSETS, scoped tool access (read-only roles like Architect can’t call terminal)
  • prior_stages(), which prior artifacts get injected into this agent’s context

prior_stages() matters most here. The Architect sees the glossary and business requirements but not the Product Owner’s raw conversation, so there’s less noise for it to build on.

class ArchitectAgent(BaseSDLCAgent):
    ROLE = "architect"
    ENABLED_TOOLSETS = {"read_file", "write_file", "skill_list", "skill_view"}
    OUTPUT_SCHEMA = {
        "type": "object",
        "required": ["adrs", "component_diagram", "tech_stack"],

Three-Tier Memory System

Rather than dumping everything into one context window, the pipeline uses three tiers of memory so each agent gets the right context:

Tier 1, Project Memory (PROJECT_MEMORY.md): Written by the Domain Expert on the first turn. Contains the shared glossary, bounded contexts, and project conventions. Injected into every agent’s system prompt, verbatim. This is the shared language of the project.

Tier 2, Artifact Bundle (SQLite + in-memory): Each completed stage writes a validated JSON artifact. Agents receive only the stages listed in their prior_stages() declaration, injected as <stage-context> fence blocks. A StreamingContextScrubber strips these tags from the model’s output in real-time to prevent the agent from echoing context blocks back.

Tier 3, Kanban Blackboard (SQLite): Used by parallel development agents to coordinate without sharing message histories. Developers post task state transitions (ready → in_progress → done) and JSON comments. The parent dispatcher reads the board; individual agents never see each other’s prompts.

The development stage fans out three agents concurrently in a ThreadPoolExecutor:

The QA Auto-Fix Loop

When QA fails, most pipelines stop and wait for a human. That’s right for some failures, but many are simple to fix in one pass: a missing import, a mismatched API signature, a forgotten migration. The QA loop handles those automatically:

    classDef gate  fill:#3A1A2A,stroke:#F38BA8,color:#F38BA8
    classDef done  fill:#1A3A2A,stroke:#A6E3A1,color:#A6E3A1

    CHK -->|yes| ADV["Advance pipeline"]:::done

    CHK -->|no| GRP["Group failing tests\nby owning developer task"]:::dev
    GRP --> FIX["Re-dispatch original\ndeveloper agent per group"]:::dev
    FIX --> RE["QA re-runs"]:::qa
    RE --> ITER{"Iteration ≤ 3?"}

    ITER -->|yes| CHK
    ITER -->|no| ESC["escalated_to_hitl = true\nPause for human review"]:::gate

The key is “group by owning developer task.” Each developer wrote code under their namespace. When those tests fail, the fix goes back to that developer, not to a generic fix agent that doesn’t know the codebase structure.

# core/qa_loop.py
class QALoop:
    def run(self, qa_agent, dev_agents, workspace, db):
        for iteration in range(self.max_iterations):
            report = qa_agent.run(workspace, db)
            if report["gate_passed"]:
                return report
            failing_by_task = self._group_failures(report["failing_tests"])
            for task_id, failures in failing_by_task.items():
                dev = self._find_owner(task_id, dev_agents)
                dev.fix(failures, workspace, db)
        report["escalated_to_hitl"] = True
        return report

Three iterations has covered almost everything I’ve tested. If it needs a fourth, it’s usually a design problem, and a human should look at it.

HITL Governance: Five Modes, One Interface

Human-in-the-loop gates exist at Requirements, Architecture, Quality Gate, and Delivery. “Human in the loop” means different things in different contexts, CLI prompt for solo dev, Slack reaction for team review, webhook for enterprise approval systems. All five modes sit behind a single interface:

The AMENDED decision is what made the system usable. If a reviewer fixes an ADR or adjusts an API contract, the pipeline mutates the artifact in-place, clears downstream stages, and continues from that point. You’re not blocked waiting for the agent to regenerate something, you fix it yourself and move on. Every decision is immutably recorded with actor and rationale.

# gateway/hitl.py
class HITLGateway:
    def request_approval(self, run_id, stage, artifact) -> ApprovalResponse:
        mode = self.config.get_mode(stage)
        if mode == "cli":
            return self._cli_prompt(artifact)
        elif mode == "auto":
            return self._auto_evaluate(artifact)
        elif mode == "slack":
            return self._slack_poll(run_id, stage, artifact)
        elif mode == "webhook":
            return self._webhook_poll(run_id, stage, artifact)
        elif mode == "queue":
            return self._queue_wait(run_id, stage, artifact)

Context Compression for Long Agent Conversations

Developer agents on large projects can burn through a context window. A backend developer writing a full REST API with auth, migrations, and tests can produce 40+ turns of tool calls and responses.

ContextCompressor handles this transparently:

  1. Monitor token count after every turn
  2. When count exceeds 80% of model limit, trigger compression
  3. Run an auxiliary model (Haiku, fast, cheap) to summarize the middle turns
  4. Preserve: system prompt (head) + last 2,000 tokens (tail)
  5. Inject a structured [STAGE COMPACTION] block:
[STAGE COMPACTION — turn 18 of 34]
Resolved Requirements: user auth via JWT, PostgreSQL backend, Redis session cache
Code Written: auth/models.py, auth/routes.py, auth/middleware.py, migrations/001_users.sql
Open Questions: rate limiting strategy — defaulting to 100 req/min per user
Remaining Work: unit tests, integration tests, OpenAPI docs

The agent carries on from this summary without the full history, much as a developer picks up from a standup note. In my testing the quality after compaction was close to what it was before.

Observability: OTel Span Hierarchy

Every agent turn emits a structured JSON log to stdout:

{
  "ts": "2026-06-01T10:00:00Z",
  "run_id": "run-abc123",
  "stage": "architecture",
  "agent": "architect",
  "turn": 4,
  "tool_calls": ["read_file", "write_file"],
  "tokens_in": 8420,
  "tokens_out": 1200,
  "cost_usd": 0.042,
  "iteration_budget_used": 4,
  "iteration_budget_max": 50
}

Optional OpenTelemetry integration adds distributed tracing across the full pipeline. The OTel SDK is an optional dependency, if not installed, a _NoOpTracer silently takes over with zero performance cost:

    classDef agent    fill:#2A1A3A,stroke:#CBA6F7,color:#CBA6F7

Prompt Injection Scanning

Before creating a run ID, the system scans the input for injection attempts across six pattern families:

# core/memory.py
INJECTION_PATTERNS = [
    r"ignore (your|all) (previous|prior) instructions",
    r"\b(act as|you are now|pretend you are)\b",
    r"^system:\s",
    r"<stage-context>",
    r"\b(dan mode|developer mode|jailbreak)\b",
    r"reveal your (system )?prompt",
]

def scan_for_injection(idea: str) -> None:
    for pattern in INJECTION_PATTERNS:
        if re.search(pattern, idea, re.IGNORECASE | re.MULTILINE):
            raise PromptInjectionError(f"Input rejected: matched pattern '{pattern}'")

The scan runs before the run_id is created, no audit trail entry, no database record, no token spend.

SQLite as the Persistence Backbone

I spent about ten minutes considering PostgreSQL. Then I remembered this is a pipeline, not a web server. Concurrency is bounded, a handful of parallel developer threads. SQLite in WAL mode handles this with zero setup.

-- 7 tables in pipeline.db
CREATE TABLE pipeline_runs   (run_id, idea, config_json, status, started_at, completed_at);
CREATE TABLE stage_artifacts (run_id, stage, artifact_json, status, created_at, approved_by);
CREATE TABLE audit_log       (run_id, stage, decision, actor, rationale, timestamp);
CREATE TABLE kanban_tasks    (task_id, run_id, title, assignee, status, metadata_json);
CREATE TABLE kanban_events   (task_id, event_type, payload, timestamp);
CREATE TABLE token_usage     (run_id, stage, agent, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_usd);
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE artifact_fts USING fts5(run_id, stage, content, content='stage_artifacts');

WAL mode + jittered exponential backoff handles concurrent developer threads cleanly:

def _execute_with_retry(self, query, params=(), max_attempts=5):
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            return self.conn.execute(query, params)
        except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:
            if "database is locked" in str(e):
                time.sleep(0.05 * (2 ** attempt) + random.uniform(0, 0.01))
            else:
                raise
    raise RuntimeError("DB lock not released after max retries")

FTS5 on stage_artifacts lets you search all artifact content with a single query, find every run that mentioned a specific API endpoint or technology.

Provider Failover and Multi-Key Rate Limit Recovery

Production LLM usage at pipeline scale hits rate limits. The solution is rotating across a credential pool:

# core/agent_runtime.py
class CredentialPool:
    def __init__(self):
        self.keys = [
            v for k, v in os.environ.items()
            if re.match(r"OPENAI_API_KEY(_\d+)?$", k)
        ]
        self._idx = 0
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def next_key(self):
        with self._lock:
            key = self.keys[self._idx % len(self.keys)]
            self._idx += 1
            return key

On a 429 response, rotate to the next key and retry immediately. On 5xx, exponential backoff on the same key. On auth or context-length errors, raise immediately, retrying won’t help.

Model Selection by Role

Not all agents need the same model. The cost difference between Opus and Haiku is roughly 60x.

Role Model Reason
Architect claude-opus-4-8 Complex multi-step ADR reasoning, C4 diagramming
All developers claude-sonnet-4-6 Best cost/quality for long code generation sessions
Domain Expert, BA, PM claude-sonnet-4-6 Structured output, moderate complexity
Context Compressor claude-haiku-4-5 Fast summarization, simple task, high volume

These are configurable per-role in sdlc_config.yaml. Swapping Sonnet for everything is a reasonable budget trade.

Custom Roles Without Code

Adding a new agent role requires zero Python:

# custom_roles/data_engineer.yaml
role: data_engineer
display_name: Data Engineer
authority_statement: |
  You design ETL pipelines, data models, and stream processing architectures.
  You write production-ready PySpark, dbt, and Airflow DAGs.
max_iterations: 35
enabled_toolsets: [read_file, write_file, terminal, execute_code]
output_schema:
  type: object
  required: [pipeline_steps, schemas_created, quality_checks]
  properties:
    pipeline_steps:
      type: array
      items:
        type: object
        required: [name, source, destination, transformation]

agents/custom_loader.py walks custom_roles/*.yaml at startup and dynamically generates agent classes. Drop a YAML file in the directory, restart, and the new role is available for any StageDefinition. Teams can add roles in the language they already know.

What the CLI Looks Like

# Start a new run
python sdlc.py run "Build a FastAPI todo app with user auth and PostgreSQL"

# With auto-approval and custom config
python sdlc.py run "idea" --config sdlc_config.yaml --auto-approve

# Resume after a HITL pause or crash
python sdlc.py resume run-abc123

# Approve a gate from the CLI
python sdlc.py approve run-abc123 architecture --decision APPROVED --rationale "ADRs look solid"

# Amend an artifact before advancing
python sdlc.py approve run-abc123 requirements --decision AMENDED --amended-artifact requirements_v2.json

# Check status and costs
python sdlc.py status run-abc123
python sdlc.py cost run-abc123

# View the kanban board
python sdlc.py kanban run-abc123

# Launch the web dashboard
python sdlc.py ui --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7474

Web Dashboard

The sdlc.py ui command launches a FastAPI web server with a real-time dashboard. Pipeline runs auto-refresh every few seconds, you can track status, stage progress, and cost without touching the CLI.

The dashboard shows all runs with their current stage, status badge (Running / Completed / Failed / Paused), start time, and duration. The stat cards at the top give a live count across all states so you can see at a glance what’s in-flight.

Clicking a run opens the run detail view, a stage pipeline with clickable nodes, each revealing its artifact, kanban tasks, audit trail, and cost breakdown in tabbed panels.

The pipeline progress bar shows all 7 stages. Stages with HITL gates are marked with a ⏸ GATE label. Approved stages show who signed off (pipeline auto-approve vs. human operator) and the timestamp. The Architecture stage here was reviewed and approved via CLI with the rationale recorded.

HITL Audit Log

Every gate decision, Approved, Rejected, or Amended, is timestamped and stored. The audit log view shows the full decision history for a run:

Rejections with cli: interrupted are operator-side ctrl+C interrupts before the gate prompt completed, the pipeline pauses and re-presents the gate on the next resume. Human approvals carry the actor name and rationale string verbatim.

Kanban Blackboard

During the parallel development stage, each developer agent claims tasks from a shared kanban board backed by SQLite. The board live-updates as agents progress:

The 20 blocked tasks here reflect a provider API error (tool_results role mismatch) that stopped the development agents mid-iteration, exactly the kind of failure the checkpoint/resume system is designed to recover from.

Token Usage and Cost

Every agent turn records tokens in, tokens out, model used, and duration. The cost tab breaks this down by stage and role:

Architecture is the most expensive stage ($0.77) because it uses Claude Opus with a large context window loading all prior discovery and requirements artifacts. The Business Analyst (requirements) comes second at $0.28 for the longest wall-clock run (~10 minutes). Development registers $0 here because the agents failed before making any API calls, cost tracking is per-turn so partially-completed agent runs are fully accounted for.

What I Got Wrong (And Fixed)

Shared filesystem for parallel developers. Three agents writing to the same directory clobbered each other’s files within seconds. Fix: path-scoped namespacing, each developer owns output/<run_id>/src/<task_id>/ exclusively, with path traversal validation on every write.

Too much context injected too early. Early versions injected all prior stage artifacts into every agent. The Architect was seeing the Product Owner’s raw conversation. Context budgets burned on noise, agents hallucinated based on conversational artefacts rather than structured ones. Fix: the prior_stages() declaration, each agent gets only what it needs, as validated JSON.

No iteration budget. Without a turn limit, agents on ambiguous tasks would loop indefinitely, rewriting the same file, retrying the same tool call, asking clarifying questions to themselves. Fix: IterationBudget with role-appropriate defaults (50 turns for Architect, 30 for developers, 20 for others).

Sync SQLite under concurrent threads. Without WAL mode and retry logic, concurrent developer threads deadlocked on DB writes constantly. Fix: WAL mode at connection open, jittered exponential backoff on OperationalError.

No AMENDED path in HITL. Early gates had only APPROVED and REJECTED. Rejection meant restarting from scratch, far too heavy for “I want to tweak this one ADR.” Adding the AMENDED path required rebuilding the gate interface but it’s the feature that made the system practical.

Checkpoint and Resume

Every completed stage writes artifacts to both SQLite and disk:

output/<run_id>/
  artifacts/
    discovery.json
    requirements.json
    architecture.json
    ...
  src/
    backend/
    ui/
    devops/

On crash or manual pause, sdlc resume <run_id> reloads all completed artifacts from SQLite and starts from the first non-completed stage. No data loss, no regeneration cost for finished work.

Closing thoughts

Building this changed how I think about agentic systems. My first instinct was to give the agents as much freedom as possible: let them spawn sub-agents, share context and work out coordination themselves. For a reliable pipeline, the opposite worked better. Tight contracts, scoped context, enforced schemas and explicit coordination.

Most of the complexity isn’t in the agents. It’s in the glue: the memory tiers, the artifact contracts, the HITL gateway, the QA loop and the context compressor. Each one exists because of a specific failure in an earlier version. None of it is glamorous, and all of it is needed.

If you’re building agents for production, start with the handoffs rather than the agents. The agents themselves are the easier part.

The full codebase is at github.com/shanmuga-sundaram-n/sdlc-factory. Questions and contributions welcome.
entry.summary: Software delivery loses information at every handoff. An idea starts out clear in someone’s head, goes through six meetings, three Confluence pages and a Jira backlog nobody reads, and ends up as code that solves last quarter’s version of the problem. Even good teams lose time and detail at each boundary between product, architecture, development and QA.

entry.title: Why Most Teams Fail at Collaboration, And How Domain-Driven Design Fixes It

link.title: Why Most Teams Fail at Collaboration, And How Domain-Driven Design Fixes It

entry.content:
Here’s a bug that took three weeks to track down.

The backend team added a status column to the users table to track onboarding progress, steps 0 to 4. The frontend team read the same field as a boolean: account active or not. The data team exported it weekly and sorted users into cold, warm and hot engagement tiers.

Nobody documented any of this, because nobody thought they needed to. The column was called status, after all.

Then a badly timed migration broke the frontend and corrupted the analytics pipeline, and the on-call engineer spent three weeks digging through git history to work out why.

Collaboration failures are like that. They hide in the gap between what you think a word means and what your colleague thinks it means, and you usually find them during a production incident at 2am.

    FIELD["users.status<br/>one column,<br/>zero documentation"]:::yellow

    FIELD --> BE["Backend<br/>status = onboarding step<br/>0 · 1 · 2 · 3 · 4"]:::blue
    FIELD --> FE["Frontend<br/>status = account live?<br/>true · false"]:::blue
    FIELD --> DA["Analytics<br/>status = engagement tier<br/>cold · warm · hot"]:::blue

    BE --> OOF["💥 3-week incident<br/>Nobody was lying.<br/>Nobody was wrong.<br/>Nobody talked."]:::red

    FE --> OOF
    DA --> OOF

    OOF --> LESSON["The problem wasn't technical.<br/>It was a missing shared model."]:::dim

It’s not a people problem. It’s a structure problem.

Most managers read this as a communication failure and reach for process: more standups, mandatory documentation, a new Confluence page that everyone writes once and nobody reads again.

I’ve seen this at startups, mid-sized companies and big enterprises. Agile ceremonies don’t fix it. Retrospectives surface it but don’t solve it. That’s because it isn’t really a people or process problem. It’s a structural one.

When teams don’t share a model of the domain they work in, every handoff is a translation, and nobody realises they’re translating. People assume they speak the same language because they use the same words. They don’t.

This is what Domain-Driven Design (DDD) addresses. Eric Evans introduced the term in 2003 and the core idea is deceptively simple: the structure of your software should reflect the structure of the business. Not the structure of your database. Not the structure of your org chart from three reorgs ago. The actual domain, the problem space your business exists to solve.

What I find most useful about DDD is how seriously it takes language.

Shared language is an architecture decision

DDD calls this Ubiquitous Language. Engineers, product managers, designers and analysts all use the same vocabulary for the domain. No “we call it an order but finance calls it a transaction.” One term, one definition, used everywhere.

That includes the code.

        direction TB
        P1["PM writes: 'Purchase'"]:::red
        P2["Eng codes: 'Transaction'"]:::red
        P3["Design mocks: 'Booking'"]:::red
        P4["Analyst queries: 'Order'"]:::red
        P1 & P2 & P3 & P4 --> CHAOS["4 mental models.<br/>Nobody catches it<br/>until it breaks."]:::red
    end

    subgraph AFTER["After — one shared glossary"]
        direction TB
        G["Order<br/>─────────────────────<br/>A confirmed purchase with<br/>payment intent, owned by<br/>a Customer, containing<br/>one or more LineItems.<br/>Not a cart. Not a quote."]:::mauve
        Q1["PM"]:::yellow
        Q2["Eng"]:::yellow
        Q3["Design"]:::yellow
        Q4["Analyst"]:::yellow

When engineers name classes and methods with the business’s own words, a product manager can read the code and recognise the concepts, and an engineer can read a spec without translating it. A whole category of bugs, the ones caused by misunderstood requirements, gets much rarer.

It’s harder than it sounds. You have to resist renaming things to what you find cleaner. If the business says “Order”, the class is Order, not PurchaseRecord, TxnEntity or SaleModel.

Teams that do this tend to move faster, because what they decided and what they built stay close together.

Big models get out of hand

Almost every growing company falls into this one.

It starts simply. You have a Customer with a name, an email and maybe a billing address, and everyone uses it. Then Sales needs to add a preferred rep. Support needs to track open ticket counts. Finance needs invoice history and credit limits. Marketing wants engagement scores. Twelve months later, Customer has 60 fields, a confusing network of relationships, and a comment at the top of the file that says // DO NOT TOUCH - ask @someone before changing anything.

Nobody owns it, which means everybody does, which in practice means nobody does.

    end

    subgraph SUPPORT["Support Context  ·  Team: CX"]
        C2["Customer<br/>─────────────<br/>Open tickets<br/>Case history<br/>CSAT score<br/>SLA tier"]:::teal
    end

    subgraph FINANCE["Finance Context  ·  Team: Finance"]

    C1 -.->|"CustomerID only"| NOTE
    C2 -.->|"CustomerID only"| NOTE

DDD’s answer is the Bounded Context: an explicit, named boundary inside which a model applies. In Sales, Customer means one thing. In Finance it means something else. Both are valid, and neither leaks into the other.

The only thing they share is a stable identifier (a CustomerID) that lets them talk about the same real-world entity without needing to agree on every attribute.

It’s also a way of assigning ownership. Bounded Contexts map to teams: Sales belongs to Commerce and Finance belongs to Finance. When something breaks in Finance’s Customer model, you know whose phone to call, and the Commerce team doesn’t need to be involved.

Draw the context map

Most teams already have several contexts, whether they know it or not. The dependencies between teams exist, but nobody has written them down. You find out when something changes upstream and breaks three things downstream that nobody knew were connected.

A Context Map fixes that. It’s a diagram of your contexts and how they relate. Hand-drawn is fine.

    ACL["Anti-Corruption Layer<br/>we translate their mess<br/>so it doesn't leak in"]:::red

    ORDERS["🛒 Orders<br/>Team: Commerce<br/>— this is the core —"]:::mauve

The useful part is the relationship labels. DDD has names for the ways contexts relate:

An Anti-Corruption Layer is what you build when you have to integrate with a system that has a messy model you don’t control. You write a translation layer that converts their concepts into yours, so their chaos doesn’t leak into your clean domain. If you’ve ever written an adapter for a third-party API with bizarre field names and six levels of nesting, you’ve built an ACL without knowing what to call it.

A Shared Kernel means two teams own a small, explicitly agreed piece of the model together. Changes require coordination. Use this sparingly, shared ownership is shared risk.

A Customer/Supplier relationship is refreshingly honest. The downstream team (customer) tells the upstream team (supplier) what they need, and the upstream team tries to deliver it. Not always with perfect success, but at least it’s named.

Names help because they make conversations more precise. “We have a dependency” becomes “we’re downstream of Payments in a Customer/Supplier relationship, and they keep breaking our integration.” That’s a more productive conversation.

Your architecture mirrors your teams

Conway’s Law sounds cynical but holds up: an organisation that designs a system will produce a design that copies its own communication structure.

Teams that don’t talk produce systems with unclear interfaces between them. Teams split by technology layer (frontend, backend, database) produce a layered monolith, even if nobody planned it.

    BAD -.-> CONWAY
    GOOD -.-> CONWAY

DDD’s suggestion is to use this deliberately. If you want an architecture organised by business domain, organise the teams by business domain first and the architecture tends to follow. It’s often called the “Inverse Conway Maneuver”, and in my experience it works better than architectural governance.

Tactical patterns

The strategic side (contexts, maps, language) gets most of the attention, but DDD also has tactical patterns that give engineers a shared vocabulary for the code. You use them once the boundaries are drawn.

%%{init: {'theme': 'dark', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#313244', 'primaryTextColor': '#CDD6F4', 'primaryBorderColor': '#45475A', 'lineColor': '#A6ADC8', 'background': '#1E1E2E', 'mainBkg': '#313244', 'clusterBkg': '#24243E', 'fontFamily': 'JetBrains Mono, monospace', 'fontSize': '13px'}}}%%
classDiagram

        <<Aggregate Root>>
        +OrderId id
        +CustomerId customerId
        +OrderStatus status
        +List~LineItem~ items
        +Money total
        +place() OrderPlaced
        +cancel() OrderCancelled
        +addItem(productId, qty)
    }

    class LineItem {
        <<Entity>>
        +LineItemId id
        +ProductId productId
        +Quantity qty
        +Money unitPrice
        +subtotal() Money
    }

    class Money {
        <<Value Object>>
        +Decimal amount
        +Currency currency
        +add(Money) Money
        +equals(Money) bool
    }

    class OrderStatus {
        <<Value Object>>
        PENDING
        CONFIRMED
        SHIPPED
        CANCELLED
    }

    class OrderPlaced {
        <<Domain Event>>
        +OrderId orderId
        +CustomerId customerId
        +Money total
        +DateTime occurredAt
    }

    class OrderRepository {
        <<Repository>>
        +findById(OrderId) Order
        +save(Order) void
        +findByCustomer(CustomerId) List~Order~

    Order "1" *-- "1..*" LineItem : contains
    Order *-- Money : total
    Order *-- OrderStatus : status

    OrderRepository ..> Order : persists
    LineItem *-- Money : unitPrice

An Aggregate is a cluster of objects that change together, with a single root that controls access. In the diagram above, Order is the root. You never reach into a LineItem directly from outside, you always go through Order. That makes the consistency boundary explicit.

Value Objects are immutable. Money has no identity, a $10 value object is interchangeable with any other $10 value object of the same currency. It prevents a whole class of bugs, such as changing a price on one object and accidentally affecting another.

Domain Events record facts. OrderPlaced means something happened, past tense, immutable, true. It’s not a command. It’s not a request. Something happened and we’re recording it. This distinction matters for how teams interact with each other.

Domain events let teams stay out of each other’s way

Understanding Domain Events properly changed how I think about team autonomy. When a context publishes an event, it announces a fact without knowing or caring who’s listening. Other contexts react. There’s no direct coupling and no “we need the Notifications team’s endpoint before we can ship.”

%%{init: {'theme': 'dark', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#313244', 'primaryTextColor': '#CDD6F4', 'primaryBorderColor': '#45475A', 'lineColor': '#A6ADC8', 'background': '#1E1E2E', 'mainBkg': '#313244', 'clusterBkg': '#24243E', 'fontFamily': 'JetBrains Mono, monospace', 'fontSize': '13px'}}}%%

    participant C as Customer
    participant O as Orders<br/>(Commerce Team)
    participant B as Event Bus
    participant P as Payments<br/>(Finance Team)
    participant N as Notifications<br/>(Engagement Team)
    participant R as Reporting<br/>(Analytics Team)

    C->>O: place order
    O->>O: validate, create Order aggregate
    O-->>B: OrderPlaced { orderId, total, customerId }
    Note over O,B: Commerce ships this.<br/>Nobody else was consulted.

    B-->>P: OrderPlaced
    P->>P: charge card, record transaction
    P-->>B: PaymentSucceeded { orderId, txnId }

Notice what’s missing. Commerce never calls Notifications directly, Engagement doesn’t wait for Finance to expose an API, and Analytics doesn’t ask Commerce for order data. Everyone reacts to shared facts, so everyone can ship without scheduling around everyone else.

For me this is the real benefit for collaboration. It works as an agreement between teams: we promise to publish accurate events, and you do what you like with them.

An example

Imagine a fintech startup with three teams sharing a Rails monolith. Payments, Accounts and Reporting all work in one codebase and all write to the same Account model, which has collected 60-odd fields over 18 months. Nobody wants to touch it.

Every release needs all three teams. A Reporting query nobody remembers fails silently when Payments changes an account state transition. Any migration needs sign-off from two other teams, and releases happen every three weeks. Everyone is worn out.

Now suppose they run an Event Storming workshop: three hours, lots of sticky notes, and some heated arguments about what “account” means. They come out with three named contexts, a rough event schema, and the realisation that Reporting never needed the Account model at all. It only needed events.

Some months later they can ship much more often. The bloated Account model still exists inside the Accounts context, but cleaning it up is that team’s job, on their own timeline. Payments has a lean model, and Reporting has a read model built from events.

You Don’t Have to Do All of This at Once

DDD has a reputation for being heavyweight because people treat it as all or nothing. They see Evans’ 560-page book and either implement everything or none of it. Neither works well.

    S2["2. Shared Glossary<br/>──────────<br/>Pick your 5 most<br/>misused terms.<br/>Write definitions. Get sign-off."]:::blue

    S3["3. Context Map<br/>──────────<br/>Draw the boundaries<br/>that already exist<br/>but aren't documented."]:::mauve

    S4["4. Tactical Patterns<br/>──────────<br/>Value Objects for money.<br/>Domain Events for<br/>cross-team handoffs."]:::teal

Begin with what gives the most value for the least disruption, which for most teams is steps 1 and 2. Run an Event Storming session with domain experts and engineers in one room, mapping what actually happens in the business. Then write a glossary for the five terms that cause the most confusion in your standups.

Neither step touches your architecture, and both improve communication straight away. Add the context boundaries, tactical patterns and event-driven integration later, when they make sense.

One thing to avoid is picking up DDD vocabulary without the discipline. If half the team says Order and the other half still says Transaction, you haven’t adopted Ubiquitous Language. You’ve added jargon. The shared vocabulary is the one part I wouldn’t do halfway.

What it really gives you

The main benefit of DDD, I think, isn’t better architecture. It’s that teams trust each other faster.

With explicit boundaries, teams can rely on each other to stay inside them. With events as the handoff, no team can break another’s internals. With a shared language, you stop spending half a meeting discovering that you’ve been talking past each other.

That is what makes collaboration work at scale. It comes from structures that make the right thing easy and the wrong thing obvious, not from more process or more documentation. How you model the domain shapes how well your teams work together. Get the model right and a lot of friction goes away. Get it wrong and no amount of Agile ceremony will save you.

If you want to try it, book a two-hour Event Storming session with your team. Bring someone from product, someone from the business side, and your senior engineers. You’ll probably be surprised by how much people disagree on terms you all thought you shared.

entry.content:
I’ve read probably a dozen RAG tutorials. They all do the same thing: show you how to embed a handful of PDFs into a vector store, run a similarity search, stuff the results into a prompt, and call it a production pipeline. Then you try to use the same approach on real data, thousands of documents, mixed formats, users with messy natural language queries, and the whole thing falls apart. The answers are vague, wrong, or confidently referencing documents that have nothing to do with the question.

That gap between “works in the tutorial” and “works in production” is what this post is about. I’ve built a few of these pipelines now, and I’ve made almost every mistake there is to make, wrong chunk sizes, no overlap, skipping the re-ranker, shipping without any evaluation. I’m going to walk through the full pipeline, from chunking to evaluation, not as a sanitized tutorial, but as the thing I wish I’d had when I started building this stuff for real.

We’ll use LangChain, ChromaDB, and OpenAI throughout. If you use different tools, the concepts all transfer.

The Two Phases You Need to Separate in Your Head

Before any code, the most important mental model is that RAG is two completely separate systems that happen to share a vector database.

The indexing pipeline is offline. It runs on a schedule or when documents change. It loads your source files, chunks them, converts them to embeddings, and writes them to a vector store. Speed isn’t critical here. Correctness is.

The query pipeline is online. It runs on every user request, and it needs to be fast. It embeds the user’s question, retrieves the most relevant chunks, builds a prompt, and calls the LLM.

Keeping these two phases decoupled is the first thing most tutorials get wrong. If your indexing and querying code are tangled together, you’ll end up in situations where you can’t re-index without restarting your query service, or where a slow re-embed job blocks user requests. Treat them as separate processes from day one.

Here’s how to get your environment set up:

print(f"ChromaDB version: {chromadb.__version__}")

Run this and confirm your package versions before going further. Version mismatches between LangChain and ChromaDB have caused me more pain than any bug I’ve written myself.

Chunking: The Part I Got Wrong for Two Weeks

I’ll be direct: chunk size is the single most important decision in this entire pipeline. It took me two weeks of debugging poor retrieval quality before I realized my chunks were the problem, not my embedding model or retrieval code. I had set chunk_size=2000 thinking “more context = better” and ended up with bloated, unfocused chunks that pulled in too much noise along with the relevant content.

The intuition is simple. A chunk is the atomic unit of retrieval. When a user asks a question, the system fetches the N most relevant chunks and hands them to the LLM. If your chunks are too large, each one contains multiple topics and the similarity score gets diluted. Too small, and you end up with fragments that don’t make sense without their surrounding context.

For most use cases, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with chunk_size=1000 and chunk_overlap=200 is a solid starting point. The recursive part matters: it tries to split on paragraph breaks first, then sentence boundaries, then spaces, only falling back to raw character splits as a last resort. This means your chunks are much more likely to contain complete thoughts rather than sentences cut in half.

The overlap is non-negotiable. Without it, a concept that straddles a chunk boundary gets split in two, and whichever half gets retrieved will be missing critical context.

from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader, DirectoryLoader
from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from langchain.schema import Document
from typing import List

def load_documents(source_dir: str) -> List[Document]:
    """Load all PDF documents from a directory."""
    loader = DirectoryLoader(
        source_dir,
        glob="**/*.pdf",
        loader_cls=PyPDFLoader,
        show_progress=True
    )
    documents = loader.load()
    print(f"Loaded {len(documents)} pages from {source_dir}")
    return documents


def chunk_documents(
    documents: List[Document],
    chunk_size: int = 1000,
    chunk_overlap: int = 200
) -> List[Document]:
    """
    Split documents into overlapping chunks.

    chunk_overlap=200 ensures continuity — if a concept spans a chunk
    boundary, both chunks will contain enough context to be meaningful.
    """
    splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
        chunk_size=chunk_size,
        chunk_overlap=chunk_overlap,
        # Try these separators in order — fall back to the next if needed
        separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""],
        length_function=len,
    )

    chunks = splitter.split_documents(documents)

    print(f"Split {len(documents)} pages into {len(chunks)} chunks")
    print(f"Average chunk size: {sum(len(c.page_content) for c in chunks) // len(chunks)} chars")

    return chunks


# --- Run it ---
docs = load_documents("./docs")
chunks = chunk_documents(docs, chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200)

# Inspect a sample chunk
sample = chunks[5]
print(f"\n--- Sample Chunk ---")
print(f"Content: {sample.page_content[:300]}...")
print(f"Metadata: {sample.metadata}")

You should see chunk counts and average sizes printed out. I strongly recommend inspecting a handful of sample chunks manually before proceeding. If your chunks look like they’re cutting off mid-sentence constantly, drop the chunk_size or double-check that your separator list is actually matching your document structure.

One more thing I wish someone had told me: always print the average chunk size after splitting. If it’s dramatically smaller than your target (say, you set 1000 but average is 400), your documents are full of very short paragraphs and you probably need to reconsider your separator strategy.

Embeddings and the Vector Store: Boring but Critical

This part feels like plumbing, and it kind of is. But bad plumbing causes leaks.

The premise is that semantically similar text produces vectors that are geometrically close in high-dimensional space. “How does attention work?” and “Explain the self-attention mechanism” don’t share many words, but their embeddings will be very close because they mean the same thing. That’s the whole trick.

I use text-embedding-3-large for anything where quality matters. It’s more expensive than text-embedding-3-small, but for a knowledge base application the quality difference is real and the cost per query is still small. For high-volume applications where you’re embedding millions of documents and running thousands of queries a day, text-embedding-3-small is worth benchmarking.

from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
from langchain_chroma import Chroma
import chromadb

def build_vector_store(
    chunks: List[Document],
    persist_directory: str = "./chroma_db",
    collection_name: str = "knowledge_base"
) -> Chroma:
    """
    Embed all document chunks and store them in ChromaDB.

    Uses text-embedding-3-large for best retrieval quality.
    Falls back gracefully if the store already exists.
    """

    # Initialize the embedding model
    # text-embedding-3-large: 1536 dims, excellent quality
    # text-embedding-3-small: cheaper, good for high-volume apps
    embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings(
        model="text-embedding-3-large",
        dimensions=1536
    )

    # Check if vector store already exists to avoid re-embedding
    if Path(persist_directory).exists():
        print(f"Loading existing vector store from {persist_directory}")
        vector_store = Chroma(
            collection_name=collection_name,
            embedding_function=embeddings,
            persist_directory=persist_directory
        )
    else:
        print(f"Building new vector store with {len(chunks)} chunks...")

        # Chroma.from_documents handles embedding + storing in one call
        vector_store = Chroma.from_documents(
            documents=chunks,
            embedding=embeddings,
            collection_name=collection_name,
            persist_directory=persist_directory,
        )
        print(f"Vector store built and persisted to {persist_directory}")

    # Verify the store
    count = vector_store._collection.count()
    print(f"Vector store contains {count} vectors")

    return vector_store


# --- Build it ---
vector_store = build_vector_store(chunks)

In production, documents change. People update wikis, replace PDFs, add new reports. You don’t want to re-embed your entire corpus every time a single file changes. The incremental indexing pattern below handles this with a simple content hash:

import hashlib
from datetime import datetime

def get_document_hash(doc: Document) -> str:
    """Generate a stable hash for a document chunk based on its content."""
    return hashlib.md5(doc.page_content.encode()).hexdigest()

def upsert_documents(
    vector_store: Chroma,
    new_chunks: List[Document]
) -> dict:
    """
    Add only new/changed documents to an existing vector store.
    Avoids re-embedding documents that haven't changed.
    """
    # Fetch all existing document IDs from the store
    existing = vector_store._collection.get(include=["metadatas"])
    existing_hashes = {
        meta.get("content_hash")
        for meta in existing["metadatas"]
        if meta.get("content_hash")
    }

    # Filter to only chunks we haven't seen before
    new_docs = []
    for chunk in new_chunks:
        content_hash = get_document_hash(chunk)
        if content_hash not in existing_hashes:
            # Stamp the chunk with its hash for future deduplication
            chunk.metadata["content_hash"] = content_hash
            chunk.metadata["indexed_at"] = datetime.now().isoformat()
            new_docs.append(chunk)

    if new_docs:
        vector_store.add_documents(new_docs)
        print(f"Added {len(new_docs)} new chunks to the vector store")
    else:
        print("No new documents to index — everything is up to date")

    return {"added": len(new_docs), "skipped": len(new_chunks) - len(new_docs)}

The first time you run this on a large corpus, embedding takes a while. Budget accordingly. On 10,000 chunks with text-embedding-3-large, expect roughly 2-3 minutes and a few dollars in API costs.

Retrieval: Where Most Pipelines Silently Die

Here’s what I mean by “silently.” A naive similarity search will almost always return something. The chunks it returns will usually be topically related to the query. The LLM will usually produce a fluent, confident answer. The problem is that the answer might be incomplete, subtly wrong, or built on the third-best chunk rather than the most relevant one. You’ll never know unless you’re logging and measuring.

The two main failure modes I’ve seen:

Redundant retrieval. You ask for k=5 chunks and get back 5 chunks that all say essentially the same thing. You’ve used your entire context window on one perspective of the topic and left out everything else.

Unfocused retrieval in multi-domain knowledge bases. If your vector store has documents from HR, engineering, finance, and legal all mixed together, a query about “approval process” might retrieve chunks from three different departments when the user only cared about one.
